---
title: "Chapter 8: Numerical optimisation"
date: today
---

The exercises take three fits that go wrong: the growth curve of loblolly pines with
complete pooling (Exercise 1, from Exercise 1 of the Chapter 7 practical), a Gamma model of
the body masses of Adelie penguins (Exercise 2) and the REML fits of a simulation of the
variance among sites (Exercise 3, from Exercise 5 of the Chapter 7 practical). Each exercise is a
full diagnosis in four steps: the **symptom**, a fit from plausible starting values that
reports convergence code 0; the **diagnosis**, with the checks of the theory; the
**remedy**; and the **confirmation** that the remedy found the maximum. All three exercises
are the core of the practical. Work through the first exercise, which is worked in full on
this page, before trying the other two. The ideas and tools are introduced in the
[Chapter 8 theory](../Theory.qmd).

As in the theory, every model is written and fitted with the packages RTMB and RTMBdist.
Exercise 1 also uses the package DEoptim for differential evolution, which you need to
install once with `install.packages("DEoptim")`; we call its functions with the prefix
`DEoptim::`, without attaching the package. Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second:

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)
```

# Exercise 1: Growth of loblolly pines

The data set `Loblolly` of base R contains the heights of 14 loblolly pines (*Pinus taeda*),
each measured at the ages of 3, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 years, 84 measurements in total, with
the heights in feet. In
[Exercise 1 of the Chapter 7 practical](../../Chapter_7/Practicals/no_solution.qmd) we
described all the trees with one growth curve (complete pooling) and a
[Normal](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-normal) observation model,

$$
H_i\sim\operatorname{Normal}\left(h(t_i),\,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}\right),
\qquad
h(t)=A\left(1-e^{-k(t-t_0)}\right),
$$

where $H_i$ is the height of measurement $i$ at the age $t_i$, $A$ is the asymptote (ft),
$k$ is the rate at which the curve approaches it (1/year), $t_0$ is the age at which the
curve crosses zero height (years), and $\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}$ is the standard deviation of
the heights around the curve (ft). The asymptote, the rate and the standard deviation are
optimised on the log scale. Chapter 7 read its starting values from a plot of the data, and
the fit reached the maximum. Here we start from another reading of the same plot.

1. Fit the model as in Chapter 7, from the starting values $A=80$ ft, $k=0.05$/year,
   $t_0=2$ years and $\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}=2$ ft. Then fit it from the same values with
   $k=0.1$/year, a curve that reaches 63% of its asymptote 10 years after $t_0$ instead of
   20 years, which is just as plausible a reading of the plot. Compare the convergence codes,
   the minima of the NLL and the estimates on the original scale. What curve does the
   second fit describe? Plot both curves over the data. See
   [A fit that stops in the wrong place](../Theory.qmd#sec-wrong-place).
2. Diagnose the second fit: its estimates on the optimised scale, the gradient at the
   solution and `sdreport()`. Calculate a slice of the log-likelihood along $\log(k)$
   through the solution, next to the same slice through the first fit, and plot both as
   relative log-likelihoods. Which checks reveal the problem, and which do not? Calculate
   the gradient at the starting values of the second fit: what does it say about the first
   step of BFGS? See [Diagnosing a fit](../Theory.qmd#sec-diagnosis) and
   [How a gradient method searches](../Theory.qmd#sec-search).
3. Fit the model from 20 sets of random starting values within a box of plausible values:
   $A$ from 30 to 300 ft, $k$ from 0.005 to 0.5/year, $t_0$ from $-5$ to 5 years and
   $\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}$ from 0.5 to 20 ft, drawn uniformly on the optimised scales (set
   seed 811 before the loop). Where did the fits end, which curve does each end point
   describe, and how many reached the lowest NLL? Restart BFGS from the best fit. See
   [Starting values and multiple starts](../Theory.qmd#sec-multistart).
4. Fit the model from the second set of starting values of question 1 with `nlminb()`.
   Then search the box of question 3 with differential evolution, with
   `DEoptim::DEoptim()`, 40 members and 200 generations (set seed 812), and refine its best
   member with BFGS. Do both reach the minimum of question 3? See
   [Other local optimisers](../Theory.qmd#sec-local-optimisers) and
   [Global search](../Theory.qmd#sec-global).
5. Confirm the best fit with the gradient and `sdreport()`, and compare its estimates with
   those of Chapter 7. What would you report about the fits of this exercise? See
   [A recipe for a difficult fit](../Theory.qmd#sec-recipe).

## Solution

### Question 1

We load the data and keep the age and the height of each measurement; this model does not
need the tree. The NLL is the one of Chapter 7:

```{r}
# Loblolly pines (see ?Loblolly), as an ordinary data frame.
data(Loblolly, package = "datasets")
pines = as.data.frame(Loblolly)

# List of data: the age (years) and the height (ft) of each measurement.
pine_data = list(age = pines$age, height = pines$height)

# Negative log-likelihood with one growth curve for all the trees (complete pooling).
pooled_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  A = exp(log_A)
  k = exp(log_k)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  # Expected height at the age of each measurement.
  mu = A * (1 - exp(-k * (age - t0)))
  -sum(dnorm(x = height, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}
```

We process the NLL with the starting values of Chapter 7 and fit it. The second fit uses
the same object, with its starting values on the optimised scales given to `optim()`:

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Process the NLL with the starting values of Chapter 7, and fit it.
pine_start = list(log_A = log(80), log_k = log(0.05), t0 = 2, log_sd_obs = log(2))
pooled_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(pooled_nll, pine_data), pine_start, silent = TRUE)
pooled_fit = optim(
  par = pooled_obj$par,
  fn = pooled_obj$fn,
  gr = pooled_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)

# The same starting values with k = 0.1/year, on the optimised scales.
fast_start = c(log_A = log(80), log_k = log(0.1), t0 = 2, log_sd_obs = log(2))
fast_fit = optim(par = fast_start, fn = pooled_obj$fn, gr = pooled_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
```

A small function returns the estimates of a fit on the original scale, so that we can
compare the two fits in one table:

```{r}
# Estimates on the original scale: A and sd_obs in ft, k in 1/year, t0 in years.
pine_estimates = function(fit) {
  c(
    A = exp(fit$par[["log_A"]]),
    k = exp(fit$par[["log_k"]]),
    t0 = fit$par[["t0"]],
    sd_obs = exp(fit$par[["log_sd_obs"]])
  )
}

# Convergence code, minimum of the NLL and estimates of the two fits.
signif(rbind(
  chapter_7 = c(convergence = pooled_fit$convergence, nll = pooled_fit$value,
                pine_estimates(pooled_fit)),
  fast_rate = c(convergence = fast_fit$convergence, nll = fast_fit$value,
                pine_estimates(fast_fit))
), 4)

# Root mean square of the heights (ft).
sqrt(mean(pine_data$height^2))
```

Both fits report convergence code 0. The first reaches the estimates of Chapter 7, with a
minimum of the NLL of 162.82. The second stops at 425.49, 263 units higher, with an
asymptote of about $1.5\times10^{-8}$ ft and a rate of about $3.6\times10^{-6}$/year. Its
curve is practically zero at every age, and its standard deviation, 38.3 ft, is the root
mean square of the heights: the spread of the 84 heights around a curve of zero. This is
the curve at zero that the CO₂ model of the theory reached from a high asymptote. The plot
shows the two curves (@fig-pine_fits):

```{r}
#| label: fig-pine_fits
#| fig-cap: "Height of 14 loblolly pines against age, with the curve of the fit from the starting values of Chapter 7 (solid line) and of the fit from the start with k = 0.1/year (dashed line, at zero)."
# Growth curve: asymptote A, rate k and age t0 at which the height is zero.
growth = function(t, A = 1, k = 1, t0 = 0) {
  A * (1 - exp(-k * (t - t0)))
}

# Measurements, and the curves of the two fits.
chapter_7_est = pine_estimates(pooled_fit)
fast_est = pine_estimates(fast_fit)
plot(height ~ age, data = pine_data, ylim = c(0, 65), xlab = "Age (years)",
     ylab = "Height (ft)")
curve(growth(x, A = chapter_7_est[["A"]], k = chapter_7_est[["k"]], t0 = chapter_7_est[["t0"]]),
      add = TRUE, col = "#D55E00")
curve(growth(x, A = fast_est[["A"]], k = fast_est[["k"]], t0 = fast_est[["t0"]]),
      add = TRUE, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Starting values of Chapter 7", "Start with k = 0.1/year"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "black"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

### Question 2

We look at the solution on the optimised scales, the gradient there and `sdreport()`. The
object has been evaluated at many points, so we pass the values of this fit to
`sdreport()` with `par.fixed`, as in the theory:

```{r}
# The solution on the optimised scales, and the gradient there.
fast_fit$par
pooled_obj$gr(fast_fit$par)

# sdreport() at the values of this fit.
fast_sd = sdreport(pooled_obj, par.fixed = fast_fit$par)
fast_sd
```

On the optimised scales, $\log(A)$ is about $-18$ and $\log(k)$ about $-12.5$: both
parameters ran towards zero, which lies at $-\infty$ on the log scale. The gradient is tiny
(its largest element, for $\log(\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}})$, is about $5\times10^{-6}$), so the
gradient alone does not reveal the problem. `sdreport()` does: the Hessian is not positive
definite (its element `pdHess` is `FALSE`: the NLL does not curve upwards in every direction
from this point, as it does at a minimum) and no standard error can be calculated.

The slice fixes the other three parameters where each fit stopped and varies the rate
between 0.02 and 0.08/year, with a `for` loop over `pooled_obj$fn()`. We draw each slice
relative to the log-likelihood where its fit stopped:

```{r}
#| label: fig-pine_slices
#| fig-cap: "Slices of the relative log-likelihood along the rate k, through the fit from the starting values of Chapter 7 (solid line) and through the fit from the start with k = 0.1/year (dashed line); the other parameters are fixed where each fit stopped."
# Slices along log(k) through the two fits: the other parameters stay where each fit stopped.
log_k_grid = seq(from = log(0.02), to = log(0.08), length.out = 301)
slice_chapter_7 = rep(NA, times = length(log_k_grid))
slice_fast = rep(NA, times = length(log_k_grid))
for (i in seq_along(log_k_grid)) {
  par_chapter_7 = pooled_fit$par
  par_chapter_7[["log_k"]] = log_k_grid[i]
  par_fast = fast_fit$par
  par_fast[["log_k"]] = log_k_grid[i]
  # Relative log-likelihood: the difference from the log-likelihood where the fit stopped.
  slice_chapter_7[i] = -pooled_obj$fn(par_chapter_7) + pooled_fit$value
  slice_fast[i] = -pooled_obj$fn(par_fast) + fast_fit$value
}

# Both slices against the rate, on a logarithmic axis.
plot(exp(log_k_grid), slice_chapter_7, type = "l", log = "x", ylim = c(-20, 2),
     col = "#D55E00", xlab = "Rate, k (1/year)", ylab = "Relative log-likelihood")
lines(exp(log_k_grid), slice_fast, lty = 2)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Starting values of Chapter 7", "Start with k = 0.1/year"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "black"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

The slice through the first fit has a sharp peak at the estimate of the rate, 0.039/year
(sharp because the asymptote and $t_0$ stay fixed, so a small change of the rate moves the
whole curve away from the data). The slice through the second fit is flat: when the
asymptote is practically zero, the curve stays at zero whatever the rate, so the NLL does not depend on $k$. The same holds for
$t_0$, and for the asymptote itself over many orders of magnitude, because a curve of
$10^{-8}$ ft and one of $10^{-2}$ ft are both zero compared with the heights. These flat
directions are why the Hessian is not positive definite. So the estimates on the optimised
scales, `sdreport()` and the slice reveal the problem, and the gradient and the convergence
code do not.

How did the search get there? The gradient at the starting values of the second fit is:

```{r}
# Gradient at the starting values with k = 0.1/year.
pooled_obj$gr(fast_start)
```

Its elements are large, from hundreds to thousands. With $k=0.1$/year the curve lies well above the
heights of the middle ages, and with a standard deviation of 2 ft every such difference
weighs heavily in the NLL. The first step of BFGS goes along the negative gradient
([theory](../Theory.qmd#sec-search)), so it starts with a change of thousands of units in
$\log(A)$. The line search shortens the step until the NLL falls, and the first point where
it falls already has an asymptote of practically zero: a curve of zero with a large standard
deviation describes the heights better than the starting curve with $\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}=2$
ft. From there no slope leads back.

### Question 3

The box is given on the optimised scales, in the order of the parameters of `pooled_obj`.
The loop draws one set of starting values with `runif()` in each repetition, fits the model
from it and stores the minimum of the NLL, the convergence code and the estimates on the
optimised scales; the seed is set once, before the loop:

```{r}
# Box of plausible starting values on the optimised scales: log asymptote, log rate,
# age at zero height and log standard deviation.
start_lower = c(log(30), log(0.005), -5, log(0.5))
start_upper = c(log(300), log(0.5), 5, log(20))

# 20 fits from random starting values within the box.
n_starts = 20
multi_results = data.frame(
  nll = rep(NA, n_starts),
  convergence = NA,
  log_A = NA, log_k = NA, t0 = NA, log_sd_obs = NA
)
set.seed(811)
for (i in 1:n_starts) {
  start = runif(4, min = start_lower, max = start_upper)
  names(start) = names(pooled_obj$par)
  fit = optim(par = start, fn = pooled_obj$fn, gr = pooled_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  multi_results[i, ] = c(fit$value, fit$convergence, fit$par)
}

# Where the 20 fits ended: minimum of the NLL (rounded) against the convergence code.
table(nll = round(multi_results$nll, 1), convergence = multi_results$convergence)
```

All 20 fits report code 0, but only 5 reach the lowest NLL, 162.8. The others end in three
places. Twelve stop at the curve at zero of question 1 (425.5). Two stop at 373.1, with the
rate run towards infinity, which makes the curve a constant; the estimates on the
optimised scales show that its asymptote is the mean of the heights:

```{r}
# Estimates of the fits that ended at 373.1, and the mean of the heights (ft).
multi_results[round(multi_results$nll, 1) == 373.1, ]
mean(pine_data$height)
```

The asymptote of these fits is $e^{3.477}\approx32.4$ ft, the mean of the 84 heights, and
$\log(k)$ is about 22. The last fit (551.2) ran far away. These are the failures of the
theory again: the curve at zero, the constant curve and a search that runs away. We
restart BFGS from the best of the 20 fits:

```{r}
# Restart BFGS from the best of the 20 fits.
best = which.min(multi_results$nll)
best_start = unlist(multi_results[best, names(pooled_obj$par)])
best_fit = optim(par = best_start, fn = pooled_obj$fn, gr = pooled_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
c(convergence = best_fit$convergence, nll = best_fit$value)
```

The restart stays at 162.82, the minimum of the first fit of question 1. Five of 20 starts
is a quarter, so in this model a single fit from random starting values in this box fails
more often than not; the agreement of five fits on the same minimum, with nothing lower, is
evidence that it is the global minimum.

### Question 4

`nlminb()` takes the starting values, the NLL and the gradient of the same object:

```{r}
# nlminb() from the start with k = 0.1/year.
fast_nlminb = nlminb(start = fast_start, objective = pooled_obj$fn, gradient = pooled_obj$gr)
fast_nlminb[c("objective", "convergence", "message", "evaluations")]
```

From the starting values at which BFGS stopped at the curve of zero, `nlminb()` reaches the
minimum of 162.82, because it controls the length of its steps differently and does not
make the long first step of BFGS. Differential evolution needs no starting values, only the
box:

```{r}
# Differential evolution within the box of question 3.
set.seed(812)
pine_de = DEoptim::DEoptim(
  fn = pooled_obj$fn,
  lower = start_lower,
  upper = start_upper,
  control = DEoptim::DEoptim.control(NP = 40, itermax = 200, trace = FALSE)
)
c(nll = pine_de$optim$bestval, evaluations = pine_de$optim$nfeval)
```

Its best member reaches the minimum as well, after 8,040 evaluations of the NLL. We refine
it with BFGS, giving the elements of the best member the names of the parameters:

```{r}
# Refine the best member with BFGS.
de_start = pine_de$optim$bestmem
names(de_start) = names(pooled_obj$par)
pine_de_fit = optim(par = de_start, fn = pooled_obj$fn, gr = pooled_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
c(convergence = pine_de_fit$convergence, nll = pine_de_fit$value)
```

BFGS stops at once at 162.82. Multiple starts, `nlminb()` and differential evolution all
reach the same minimum, which none of the searches has gone below.

### Question 5

We diagnose the restart of question 3 as in the theory and compare its estimates with
those of Chapter 7:

```{r}
# Largest absolute gradient and sdreport() at the best fit.
max(abs(pooled_obj$gr(best_fit$par)))
best_sd = sdreport(pooled_obj, par.fixed = best_fit$par)
best_sd$pdHess
summary(best_sd)

# Estimates on the original scale: the best fit and the fit from the start of Chapter 7.
rbind(best = pine_estimates(best_fit), chapter_7 = pine_estimates(pooled_fit))
```

The gradient is close to zero, the Hessian is positive definite and the standard errors are
small, so the best fit passes every check. Its estimates agree with those of Chapter 7: an
asymptote of 102 ft, a rate of 0.039/year, $t_0=2.06$ years and a standard deviation of
1.68 ft. The fit of Chapter 7 had found the maximum; the second start of question 1 had
not.

In a report we give the estimates of the best fit with their standard errors, and say how
we know that it is the maximum: BFGS from one plausible start stopped at a curve of zero
with code 0, 5 of 20 random starts reached the same minimum and none went lower, and
`nlminb()` and differential evolution confirmed it.

# Exercise 2: Body mass of Adelie penguins

The data set `penguins` of the package `datasets` (R 4.5.0 and later) contains the body
masses, in grams, of adult penguins of three species near Palmer Station, Antarctica. We
fit a [Gamma](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-gamma) model with shape $k$ and rate
$r$, the model of the tree volumes in Exercise 4 of the
[Chapter 4 practical](../../Chapter_4/Practicals/no_solution.qmd), to the body masses of
the 151 Adelie penguins whose mass was recorded,

$$
X_i \sim \operatorname{Gamma}(k, r), \qquad E[X_i]=\frac{k}{r},
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\frac{k}{r^2},
$$

where $X_i$ is the body mass of penguin $i$, with $\log(k)$ and $\log(r)$ as the
parameters. Started at the method-of-moments estimates, the fit to the masses in grams
stops after a single step and reports convergence code 0. Load the data with
`data(penguins, package = "datasets")`, keep the Adelie penguins and remove the one penguin
whose mass is missing (`NA`).

1. Fit the Gamma model to the masses in grams with `dgamma()`, starting at the
   method-of-moments estimates $\hat k=\overline x^2/\hat\sigma^2$ and $\hat r=\overline x/\hat\sigma^2$, where $\overline x$ is the
   mean of the masses and $\hat\sigma^2$ their empirical variance with divisor $n$. Before
   the fit, check that `fn` and `gr` return ordinary numbers at the starting values. Report the
   convergence code, the numbers of evaluations of `fn` and `gr`, and the shape at the start
   and at the end of the search. What do the counts say about the search? Hint: the NLL is
   the one of Exercise 4 of the Chapter 4 practical. The element `counts` of the result of
   `optim()` is explained in [Exact and approximate gradients](../Theory.qmd#sec-gradients);
   BFGS evaluates the gradient at its starting values and again after every step that
   counts as progress, and the rule that decides which steps count is in
   [Stopping rules and convergence codes](../Theory.qmd#sec-stopping).
2. Diagnose the fit with the gradient at the solution and a refit from the solution. How
   much lower is the NLL at the end of the refit? Then use the stopping rule of BFGS to
   explain why the first search stopped: compare the decrease of the NLL in its single step
   with the smallest decrease that counts as progress. Hint: the checks are those of
   [Diagnosing a fit](../Theory.qmd#sec-diagnosis). The smallest decrease that counts as
   progress is the formula in
   [Stopping rules and convergence codes](../Theory.qmd#sec-stopping), where
   $|{-\ell(\boldsymbol\theta)}|$ is the NLL at the start of the step, `obj$fn(obj$par)`,
   and `reltol` is `sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)`.
3. Try three remedies, each from the method-of-moments estimates: (a) the masses in
   kilograms; (b) the parameterisation with the mean $\mu=k/r$ and the shape, with
   $\log(\mu)$ and $\log(k)$ as the parameters, starting at the mean of the masses and the
   method-of-moments estimate of the shape; and (c) `nlminb()` with the masses in grams.
   Which of them reach the maximum that the refit of question 2 found? Hint: for (a),
   calculate the method-of-moments estimates again from the masses in kilograms. For (b),
   the rate is $k/\mu$; Exercise 1 of the Chapter 6 practical wrote the Gamma model with its
   mean in the same way, through `scale = mu / shape`
   ([Parameterisation](../Theory.qmd#sec-parameterisation)). For (c), see
   [Other local optimisers](../Theory.qmd#sec-local-optimisers). The minimum of the NLL in
   kilograms differs from that in grams, so compare the estimates of the shape, which has no
   units.
4. Explain why each remedy reaches the maximum. For the masses in kilograms, calculate the
   smallest decrease that counts as progress at the starting values and compare it with
   that in grams and with the decrease of the single step of question 2. Why is the NLL
   smaller in kilograms? For the parameterisation, compare the correlation of the estimates
   of $\log(k)$ and $\log(r)$ with that of the estimates of $\log(\mu)$ and $\log(k)$, both
   at the maximum. Which of the three remedies and the refit of question 2 change the
   problem that the optimiser solves, and which search the same problem again? Hint: the
   effect of the units on the log-likelihood is explained in
   [The likelihood function](../../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood) of Chapter 4. The
   correlations are `cov2cor()` of the element `cov.fixed` of `sdreport()`, as in Exercise 4
   of the Chapter 4 practical, with `par.fixed` set to the estimates at the maximum. See
   [Scaling and parameterisation](../Theory.qmd#sec-scaling).

# Exercise 3: A variance among sites at zero

In [Exercise 5 of the Chapter 7 practical](../../Chapter_7/Practicals/no_solution.qmd) we
simulated 500 hypothetical samples of the log biomass of the herb layer (biomass in g/m²)
in five quadrats at each of six sites, from a Normal model with a random intercept for each
site,

$$
u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}\left(0,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{site}}\right),
\qquad
Y_{ij}\mid u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}\left(\mu+u_j,\,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}\right),
$$

where $Y_{ij}$ is the log biomass in quadrat $i$ of site $j$, with $\mu=4$ and
$\sigma_{\mathrm{site}}=\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}=1$, and estimated the variances by REML. In
some samples the REML estimate of $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{site}}$ was practically zero. In some of
these the maximum of the likelihood lies at zero, and in others the fit stopped on its way
towards zero although the maximum lies at a positive variance. Here we tell the two cases
apart. That exercise was extra practice; if you skipped it, the code below gives you the
samples, and [Estimates at a boundary](../Theory.qmd#sec-boundaries) explains the two cases.

The code below repeats the simulation with the seed of Chapter 7, so that the samples are the
same, but fits only REML, and it keeps every sample and the result of its fit. It needs the
helper `cmb()`. As in Chapter 7, every fit starts from the values used to simulate:

```{r}
# Joint NLL of a Normal model with a random intercept for each site (Chapter 7).
site_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  log_biomass = OBS(log_biomass)
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the sites, before they are used.
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_site), log = TRUE))
  nll - sum(dnorm(x = log_biomass, mean = mu + u[site], sd = exp(log_sd_obs), log = TRUE))
}

# The design, five quadrats at each of six sites, and the values used to simulate, which
# are also the starting values of every fit. The log biomasses are placeholders.
n_sites = 6
site_index = rep(seq_len(n_sites), each = 5)
site_start = list(mu = 4, log_sd_site = log(1), log_sd_obs = log(1), u = rep(0, n_sites))
placeholder_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(site_nll, list(log_biomass = rep(0, times = 5 * n_sites), site = site_index)),
  site_start,
  random = "u",
  silent = TRUE
)

# 500 hypothetical samples (one column each) and the REML fit of each, with the mean
# integrated out together with the site deviations.
n_samples = 500
reml_samples = matrix(NA, nrow = 5 * n_sites, ncol = n_samples)
reml_results = data.frame(
  nll = rep(NA, n_samples),
  convergence = NA,
  log_sd_site = NA,
  log_sd_obs = NA
)
set.seed(751)
for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
  reml_samples[, i] = placeholder_obj$simulate(placeholder_obj$par)$log_biomass
  reml_obj = MakeADFun(
    cmb(site_nll, list(log_biomass = reml_samples[, i], site = site_index)),
    site_start,
    random = c("u", "mu"),
    silent = TRUE
  )
  reml_fit = optim(par = reml_obj$par, fn = reml_obj$fn, gr = reml_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  reml_results[i, ] = c(reml_fit$value, reml_fit$convergence, reml_fit$par)
}

# REML estimates of the variance among sites.
reml_results$var_site = exp(2 * reml_results$log_sd_site)
```
